title: Can You Use an HSA or FSA for Acupuncture? (2026 Guide)
summary: Yes, acupuncture is HSA and FSA eligible under IRS rules. See what's covered, what isn't, how insurance fits in, and how to pay with pre-tax dollars.
body_markdown:
**Yes.** Acupuncture is an eligible medical expense, so you can use pre-tax dollars from your health savings account (HSA) or flexible spending account (FSA) for it, either at the clinic or through reimbursement. IRS Publication 502 lists it directly: "You can include in medical expenses the amount you pay for acupuncture." You don't need a Letter of Medical Necessity to use your HSA for acupuncture treatment itself, though your plan may ask for a detailed receipt.


## Is acupuncture HSA and FSA eligible?


Medical expenses under IRS regulations include amounts paid for the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease, and must be primarily to alleviate or prevent a physical or mental defect or illness. Many patients use acupuncture alongside other healthcare for various conditions, to relieve symptoms of a specific medical condition or illness, such as:


- Chronic pain, including low back pain and neck pain
- Migraine and tension headache symptoms
- Osteoarthritis and joint pain symptoms
- Nausea symptoms, including nausea related to chemotherapy or pregnancy


Because[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) names acupuncture specifically, it's eligible for a health savings account, a flexible spending account, and an HRA. Your employer's plan documents can still limit what a flexible spending account or HRA allows for reimbursement, so check your plan if you're unsure.


## What eligible expenses can your HSA or FSA cover for acupuncture?


- Acupuncture treatment sessions from a licensed acupuncturist
- Initial evaluations and follow-up visits that are part of your treatment
- Electroacupuncture provided during a session
- Copays, deductibles, and coinsurance if your health insurance includes acupuncture benefits
- Acupuncture provided by a doctor, physician, or chiropractor as medical treatment


Acupuncture costs vary by location and acupuncture provider. Whatever portion your health plan doesn't pick up is eligible for reimbursement from your health savings account or flexible spending account.


## Which related medical treatments usually aren't eligible?


Expenses that are merely beneficial to general well-being don't qualify, so these usually need a Letter of Medical Necessity, or aren't eligible at all:


- **Herbal medicines and supplements.** Eligible only if a medical practitioner prescribes or recommends them to treat a specific medical condition, which is what a[Letter of Medical Necessity](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-letter-of-medical-necessity) documents.
- **Essential oils, teas, and relaxation products.** These are generally personal expenses.
- **Wellness-only services.** Sessions for general relaxation, rather than a diagnosed condition, may not qualify.


## What documentation do you need for reimbursement?


In most cases, a detailed receipt is enough for medical expenses related to acupuncture to be reimbursed. It should list the provider's name, the date of service, the service (acupuncture), and the amount.


Some flexible spending account administrators may also ask for documentation of a medical diagnosis, or a note showing the treatment was prescribed or recommended by your physician or another healthcare provider, especially if the service could look like general wellness rather than medically necessary health care. Maintain detailed records, and if a reimbursement request is denied, contact your plan administrator to ask what's missing before you resubmit for reimbursement.


## Does health insurance cover acupuncture?


Coverage varies widely. Some health plans include a limited number of sessions for specific conditions, and Medicare Part B covers acupuncture for chronic low back pain under certain conditions. Many plans don't include it at all. Sessions your insurance doesn't include, copays and coinsurance, out-of-network acupuncturists, and visits beyond your plan's limit are all eligible for reimbursement from a health savings account or flexible spending account.


## Health care FSA vs. HSA benefits for acupuncture


- **HSA funds roll over** , so a health savings account works well for a long course of treatment, and the money stays with you if you change jobs.
- **Flexible spending account funds expire** at the end of your plan year, apart from any carryover or grace period. If you have[unused funds](https://www.withflex.com/blog/use-or-lose-fsa-expire) late in the year, acupuncture sessions are a practical way to use them.
- **Limited purpose FSAs** only allow reimbursement for dental and vision expenses, so use your health savings account for acupuncture if you have both.
- **Family members** are eligible too: either account's benefits extend to acupuncture for your spouse and dependents.


## How HSA and FSA reimbursement works for acupuncture


1. **Use your card at the acupuncture clinic.** Most acupuncture practices accept health savings account and flexible spending account cards, so there's no reimbursement step.
2. **Or submit a reimbursement request.** Send your detailed receipt to your plan administrator. Flexible spending account reimbursement usually has a deadline after the plan year ends, while HSA reimbursement can happen any time after the expense, as long as your HSA was open when you received care. Here's[how HSA and FSA reimbursement works](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-fsa-reimbursement-how-to) .
3. **Keep your documentation.** FSA administrators often ask for it, and HSA owners need it if the IRS asks. Using HSA funds for non-qualified expenses means income tax plus a 20% penalty if you're under 65.


## A comprehensive list of related eligible expenses


Acupuncture is one of many eligible expenses.[Chiropractic care](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-fsa-chiropractor) , physical therapy, over the counter medicines, first aid supplies, and transportation directly related to medical care are also eligible without an LMN, while[massage therapy](https://www.withflex.com/blog/can-you-use-hsa-fsa-for-massage) , herbal treatments, and items like an air purifier need one. Any money you contribute to a flexible spending account can go toward these, as long as you use it before the plan year ends. See our[list of 200+ FSA eligible items](https://www.withflex.com/blog/fsa-eligible-items-list) for more, or browse pain relief and recovery products in the[Flex Marketplace](https://www.withflex.com/shop) , where qualifying customers can get an LMN at checkout.
